idiom_name: clang::ast_matchers matcher DSL with MatchFinder, Rewriter and Transformer RewriteRule
implementation_notes: LibASTMatchers expresses the pattern as a composed predicate - binaryOperator(hasOperatorName("+"), hasEitherOperand(integerLiteral(equals(0)))).bind("add") - and MatchFinder owns the traversal, invoking a MatchCallback once per match with nodes addressed by their bind id; the action is the callback body, and rewriting goes through Rewriter (insert or remove text at node extents) or the Transformer library's RewriteRule, which pairs a matcher with edits. That is the pattern's full shape in C++: a rule table of matcher/action pairs and no walker written by hand. A plain RecursiveASTVisitor or a single dyn_cast wins only when the whole rule would be one node-type check, since matcher expressions cost compile time and require a LibTooling build.
code_sketch:
using namespace clang::ast_matchers;
MatchFinder finder;
finder.addMatcher(
    binaryOperator(hasOperatorName("+"),
                   hasEitherOperand(integerLiteral(equals(0))))
        .bind("add"),
    &dropZeroHandler);            // action: rewrite x + 0 to x
finder.matchAST(context);         // MatchFinder owns the walk
pitfalls: Matcher expressions are templates: a wrong child matcher (hasLHS instead of hasEitherOperand, or a missing ignoringParenImpCasts) compiles fine and silently matches nothing, so each rule needs a positive and a near-miss test.
The AST is shared and effectively immutable: rewriting goes through Rewriter source edits or a reconstructed tree, and holding raw Decl or Stmt pointers across a rewrite pass leaves stale nodes.
Match callbacks run during a single traversal, so a callback that mutates the AST or runs further matchers invalidates the traversal it is called from.

variants.name: LLVM PatternMatch and SDPatternMatch over IR and DAG nodes
variants.idiom_name: llvm::PatternMatch and llvm::SDPatternMatch matchers (m_Add, m_Value, m_Deferred), TableGen ISel patterns
variants.implementation_notes: For a tree that is not source - LLVM IR instructions or SelectionDAG nodes - llvm/Support/PatternMatch.h and CodeGen/SDPatternMatch.h provide the matcher DSL: m_Add(m_Value(X), m_Deferred(X)) binds operands and returns bool, so a pass writes if (match(I, m_Add(...))) instead of chained dyn_cast and child checks, with InstCombine as the canonical consumer. Instruction selection goes further and moves the rule table out of C++ entirely: SelectionDAG ISel patterns are written in TableGen and compiled into the matcher, so the patterns are declarative data with an explicit priority mechanism. Choose this variant when the subject is compiler IR or a DAG rather than source text, and remember the matchers are C++-level predicates, not a user-extensible rule language.
pitfalls: m_Specific binds a value before the match runs, so a repeated variable in one pattern must use m_Deferred; getting this wrong makes the pattern never match.

TableGen ISel patterns are tried bottom-up over the DAG with implicit ordering, so overlapping patterns need an explicit AddedComplexity or a more specific pattern, and a wrong rule shows up only as worse code generation in a test.
Matchers over IR are not matchers over source: they see canonicalised IR (and SDPatternMatch sees a DAG), so a shape that is obvious in source may have been folded away or split before the rule runs.
